bib.venue: Wiley book chapter (2nd ed.; edition and year not printed in the chapter text)

question: How to dimensionally model inventory (periodic snapshot, transaction, accumulating snapshot) and how to integrate data marts across a value chain via a bus architecture with conformed dimensions and facts.
contributions: Semi-additive facts and enhanced inventory facts (turns, days' supply, GMROI)
Data warehouse bus architecture and bus matrix

limits: Examples are hypothetical (60,000 products, 100 stores); no measured data.
Written around 2002 data-mart/OLAP tooling; storage figures (14-byte rows, 30 GB/year) have dated, and the SQL AVG limitation is stated for standard SQL of that time.
Accumulating snapshot deferred to Chapter 5; multiple units of measure to Chapter 5; heterogeneous products to Chapter 9.
practices: Declare grain first, then dimensions: daily inventory by product by store gives date, product, store (p.69).
Do not attach a promotion dimension to inventory snapshots; promotions attach to product movement (p.69).
Treat inventory snapshot as dense and include zero-quantity rows; cut volume by keeping recent days daily and older history weekly in a separate fact table (p.70).
Aggregate semi-additive facts over time by averaging, dividing by the count of dates, not by SQL AVG row count (p.72).
Store additive components, never ratios like GMROI (p.73).
Pair a transaction fact table with a snapshot table, since transactions alone are impractical for inventory position (p.75).
Use accumulating snapshot (one row per shipment, updated through milestones, multiple date FKs) when shipments can be reliably distinguished (p.75).
Build the bus matrix early: rows are source-aligned business processes, columns common dimensions (p.79-81).
Implement first-level data marts before consolidated ones; avoid profitability as a first mart, or allocate costs by rule of thumb if forced (p.80).
Retrofit stovepipe marts by cross-reference mapping to conformed dimensions and re-keying facts, or rebuild if grain is wrong (p.82).
Roll-up dimensions (brand) must be strict subsets of the atomic dimension (product), with identically labelled shared attributes (p.83).
Assign a dimension authority to build once in staging and publish synchronously to marts (p.85-86).
Make conformed-dimension use a business policy mandated from the top (p.86).
If full conformity is unrealistic, conform a least-common-denominator set of attributes (p.87).
Drill across with multipass SQL per mart, outer-joined on a common dimension attribute (p.77).

terms.definition: the natural, logical flow of an organization's primary activities
every day (or at some other regular time interval), we measure the inventory levels of each product and place them as separate rows in a fact table
one fact table row for each product delivery and update the row until the product leaves the warehouse
additive across some dimensions but not all (e.g. inventory levels, account balances)
gross margin return on inventory: total quantity sold x (value at latest selling price - value at cost) / (daily average quantity on hand x value at latest selling price)
multipass SQL querying each data mart separately, outer joining results on a common dimension attribute
a standard interface so separate data marts built by different groups at different times plug together via conformed dimensions and facts
business processes as rows, common dimensions as columns; the tool to create, document and communicate the bus architecture
a data mart derived from a single primary source system
a multisource mart that typically crosses business processes (e.g. profitability)
identical or strict mathematical subsets of the most granular, detailed dimension, with consistent keys, attribute names, definitions and values
group responsible for defining, maintaining, and publishing a conformed dimension or its subsets
KPIs such as revenue and profit that share definitions, equations, dimensional context and units across marts
